questions.q: Why work inside a virtual environment?
options: It isolates each project's packages so one project's versions can't break another's
questions.explain: pip installs into .venv instead of the system Python.

questions.q: Which library is used for classical machine learning in this stack?
questions.explain: NumPy is for arrays, pandas for tables, matplotlib for plots and PyTorch for neural networks.

questions.q: What is the recommended habit about notebooks and scripts?
options: Explore in a notebook, then consolidate what worked into a script
questions.explain: Scripts are version-control friendly and look like production code.

questions.q: How do you know the setup is done?
options: All five library versions print when check_stack.py runs
questions.explain: Exact versions don't matter; anything from the last few years works.

questions.q: What is the single most-checked property in ML code?
questions.explain: A dataset of 150 examples with 4 features is (150, 4); shape mismatches are the most common bug.

questions.q: What is vectorization?
options: Applying operations element-wise with the loop running in optimized C instead of Python
Converting data to vectors of text
questions.explain: The lesson's benchmark was roughly 50–100x faster than a Python loop.

questions.q: What does M.mean(axis=0) compute for a 2-row, 3-column array?
questions.explain: axis=0 goes down the columns, giving [2.5, 3.5, 4.5] for the example.

questions.q: What is the practical rule when you write a for loop over data points?
options: Look for the array operation instead
questions.explain: Training does millions of multiply-adds, so vectorization matters.

questions.q: Why set aside a test set before doing anything else?
options: To measure performance on data the model hasn't seen, and not touch it until the end
questions.explain: A model can simply memorize training data, so evaluating on it is meaningless.

questions.q: What does stratify=y do in train_test_split?
options: Keeps each class in the same proportion in both splits
questions.explain: It's used for classification.

questions.q: Why impute with the median rather than the mean?
options: The median is robust to outliers
questions.explain: SimpleImputer(strategy="median") learns per-column medians from the data it's fit on.

questions.q: What is data leakage?
options: A silent bug that makes bad models look good
questions.explain: It's the most important concept in practical ML data preparation.

questions.q: What does regression predict?
options: A number, such as a house price
questions.explain: Classification predicts categories.

questions.q: What does least squares training minimize?
options: The squared difference between predictions and actual values on the training set
questions.explain: It finds the weights w and intercept b.

questions.q: Why is linear regression the baseline of choice?
options: You can read and reason about each weight
It always has the best accuracy
questions.explain: For example each extra unit of MedInc adds about 0.449 (≈$44,900) to the prediction.

questions.q: Which two failure modes haunt every model?
questions.explain: The module introduces both after fitting a line.

questions.q: What does logistic regression do despite its name?
options: It is a classifier: a weighted sum squashed through a sigmoid into a probability, thresholded at 0.5
questions.explain: It outputs probabilities between 0 and 1.

questions.q: Why does predict_proba matter in practice?
options: '97% likely benign' supports different decisions than '51% likely benign', though predict returns 1 for both
questions.explain: Probabilities carry confidence that labels hide.

questions.q: Why is scaling done inside a pipeline for logistic regression?
options: It, like most non-tree models, cares about feature scale
questions.explain: Decision trees need no scaling and are directly inspectable.

questions.q: What does stratify=y preserve in the breast cancer split?
options: The class ratio (about 63/37) in both splits
questions.explain: The dataset has 357 benign and 212 malignant tumors.

questions.q: What distinguishes unsupervised learning?
options: It finds structure with no labels at all
It requires a test set only
questions.explain: fit_predict in the k-means example consumes only X.

questions.q: Why scale features before k-means on real data?
options: k-means is pure distance math, so scale dominates distances
questions.explain: Use StandardScaler.

questions.q: What does the elbow method look for?
options: The bend in inertia versus k where improvements level off
questions.explain: In the example, inertia drops hugely until k=4, then only marginally.

questions.q: What is true of cluster IDs?
options: They are arbitrary: only the grouping is meaningful
questions.explain: Cluster 2 this run may be cluster 0 next run.

questions.q: What does the five-seed experiment show?
options: Accuracy wobbles by 3+ points depending on the split, so a single number is partly luck
questions.explain: Same model, same data.

questions.q: How does k-fold cross-validation work?
options: Train k times, holding out a different fold each time, and report mean ± std
questions.explain: Every row is used for testing exactly once.

questions.q: Why is the scaler inside a Pipeline important for CV?
options: It's re-fit inside each fold on that fold's training portion, avoiding leakage
questions.explain: Scaling X once up front leaks test fold statistics.

questions.q: What is the cost of cross-validation?
questions.explain: cv=5 or cv=10 are standard.

questions.q: What does a scikit-learn Pipeline guarantee?
options: Preprocessing is learned only from training data, with the whole pipeline refit per CV fold
questions.explain: You literally cannot forget to re-fit the scaler per fold.

questions.q: What does pipe.predict/pipe.score do with the scaler?
questions.explain: pipe.fit runs fit_transform through each step, then fits the final model.

questions.q: What is feature engineering?
options: Deriving columns that expose the signal more directly
questions.explain: Models can only use the information you give them, in the form you give it.

questions.q: What is the standard real-world skeleton the module builds toward?
questions.explain: It handles different column types in one object.

questions.q: What two additions does a torch.Tensor have over a NumPy ndarray?
options: It can live on a GPU and it can track gradients
questions.explain: Shapes, vectorization and reductions transfer directly, using dim instead of axis.

questions.q: What does loss.backward() compute for loss = (w - 5)^2 at w = 3?
In which direction does gradient descent nudge w?
options: A small step against the gradient: w ← w − lr · grad
questions.explain: A negative gradient means loss decreases if w increases, so w increases.

questions.q: What is a neural net, under the hype?
options: Layers of linear regression with non-linear squashes between them, trained by gradient descent
questions.explain: Tensors, autograd, an MLP and the training loop are the four core ideas.

questions.q: Why does all data logic live in prepare.py, imported by both training and prediction?
options: So the exact same code path that prepared training data prepares future data
questions.explain: Divergence between those paths is where production ML bugs come from.

questions.q: What data quirk does the exploration step reveal about the target?
questions.explain: It also shows outliers such as 141 rooms per household.

questions.q: Which feature correlates most with house value?
questions.explain: Income dominates.

questions.q: What does train.py save for reuse?
questions.explain: predict.py loads it to predict for new districts.

questions.q: What is bagging?
options: Training many copies of a model on bootstrap samples (drawn with replacement) and averaging predictions
questions.explain: It mostly tames variance, not bias.

questions.q: What extra randomness does a random forest add?
options: Only a random subset of features is considered at each split
questions.explain: This decorrelates the trees.

questions.q: What does max_features="sqrt" mean?
options: Each split considers about the square root of the number of features
questions.explain: It's the default for classification.

questions.q: Why does a single decision tree overfit easily?
options: It memorizes noise along with signal
questions.explain: Ensembles combine many models so their errors average out.

questions.q: How does boosting differ from a random forest?
options: Boosting builds trees sequentially, each correcting the ensemble's errors; forests build independent trees and average
questions.explain: Boosting is usually the strongest technique for tabular data.

questions.q: What is a weak learner here?
options: A shallow tree (e.g. max_depth=3) adding a small learning_rate-scaled correction
questions.explain: The ensemble solves the problem collectively over many small steps.

questions.q: What does early stopping do in XGBoost?
options: Stops adding trees once validation loss stalls
questions.explain: E.g. 143 of 2000 trees used.

questions.q: What do subsample and colsample_bytree do?
options: Add bagging-style row and column subsampling per tree to fight overfitting
questions.explain: XGBoost is boosting plus a bit of bagging.

questions.q: Why is a random train_test_split invalid for time series?
options: It would let the model train on future days and be tested on earlier ones
questions.explain: Split by time instead, or use TimeSeriesSplit.

questions.q: Why write shift(1).rolling(7).mean() instead of rolling(7).mean()?
options: So the feature for day t only uses data available before day t
questions.explain: An un-shifted window silently includes today's own target value, the most common time-series ML bug.

questions.q: What do lag features capture?
options: Earlier values of the series, such as the value 1, 2 or 7 days ago
questions.explain: They are created with shift(lag).

questions.q: What does TimeSeriesSplit do?
options: Multiple folds that each still respect time order
questions.explain: Training windows grow with each fold.

questions.q: What is a bag of words?
options: Each document as a vector of word counts, with word order thrown away
questions.explain: CountVectorizer builds the vocabulary and counts.

questions.q: What problem does TF-IDF address?
options: Raw counts over-value words that are frequent everywhere; it rescales by how distinctive a word is across the corpus
questions.explain: It down-weights common words.

questions.q: Why call tfidf.transform (not fit_transform) on the test set?
options: To reuse the training vocabulary and IDF
questions.explain: Fitting on test data would leak.

questions.q: What does the lesson do with the classifier's coefficients?
options: Inspect the highest and lowest to see the most 'space' and most 'baseball' words
questions.explain: It reveals what the model actually learned.

questions.q: Why are CNNs better than plain MLPs for images?
options: They exploit spatial structure instead of treating pixels as a flat list
questions.explain: Nearby pixels are related.

questions.q: What shape is a FashionMNIST image tensor?
questions.explain: One grayscale channel; color photos would have 3.

questions.q: What does nn.MaxPool2d(2) do?
questions.explain: 28×28 becomes 14×14, then 7×7.

questions.q: What does the final layer output?
questions.explain: CrossEntropyLoss takes logits.

questions.q: What is transfer learning?
options: Reusing a network pretrained on a huge dataset and adapting it to a smaller task
questions.explain: It needs far less data and training time.

questions.q: How many parameters train when only the new 3-class head is trainable?
questions.explain: The other ~11.2M parameters stay frozen.

questions.q: Why must you use the same normalization statistics as pretraining?
options: Differently scaled images shift activations away from the ranges the filters were tuned for, destroying the benefit
questions.explain: Use weights.transforms().

questions.q: What does requires_grad = False do?
options: Freezes a weight so it isn't updated
questions.explain: It freezes the backbone.

questions.q: What does permutation importance measure?
options: The drop in performance when a feature's values are shuffled, breaking its relationship to the target
How often a feature is used for splitting
questions.explain: It is model-agnostic and computed on held-out data.

questions.q: Why can feature_importances_ be misleading?
options: It counts how often a feature is used for splitting, which can be biased toward high-cardinality features
questions.explain: Permutation importance is computed on X_test instead.

questions.q: What does partial dependence show that importance does not?
options: The shape of the relationship between a feature and the prediction
questions.explain: For MedInc, value rises steeply then flattens: diminishing returns.

questions.q: Why does interpretability matter in credit, healthcare and hiring?
options: Interpretable models are always more accurate
A model that predicts well but can't explain why is a liability in regulated domains
questions.explain: It's also a debugging aid everywhere else.

questions.q: Why apply resampling only to the training set?
options: Resampling can't run on test data
The test set must stay a faithful sample of real-world class proportions for an honest estimate
questions.explain: Never resample X_test.

questions.q: What does SMOTE do?
questions.explain: RandomOverSampler duplicates; RandomUnderSampler drops majority rows.

questions.q: What trade-off do the resampling results show versus the baseline?
options: Recall rises sharply (0.18 → ~0.8) while precision falls
questions.explain: Baseline precision 0.833 with recall 0.179.

questions.q: Why choose a decision threshold deliberately?
options: scikit-learn's default of 0.5 may not suit the cost of errors
questions.explain: ROC and precision-recall curves evaluate across all thresholds.

questions.q: What is the idea of user-based collaborative filtering?
options: Find users with similar rating patterns and recommend what they liked that you haven't seen
questions.explain: The lesson uses cosine similarity.

questions.q: How sparse are real recommender datasets typically?
questions.explain: Most users have rated only a handful of items.

questions.q: What does matrix factorization learn?
options: A small vector of latent factors per user and item whose dot product approximates observed ratings
questions.explain: Neighborhood methods scale poorly and struggle with sparsity.

questions.q: What fallback does predict_rating use when no neighbor rated the item?
questions.explain: It avoids returning nothing.

questions.q: Why does the churn project use average_precision for the search score?
options: It suits an imbalanced (~80/20) classification problem
It's the default for all models
questions.explain: RandomizedSearchCV scores with it.

questions.q: What does scale_pos_weight do in XGBoost here?
questions.explain: Candidates include 1, 3 and 4.

questions.q: What does ColumnTransformer allow?
options: Scaling numeric columns and one-hot encoding the categorical column in one preprocessing step
questions.explain: has_addon is passed through unchanged with remainder="passthrough".

questions.q: Which factors drive churn in the simulated data?
options: Tenure, contract type and support tickets
questions.explain: Month-to-month contracts and tickets raise churn; tenure lowers it.

questions.q: What is self-attention?
options: Every position in a sequence looks at every other position and decides how much to attend to it
questions.explain: It is the core idea of the transformer.

questions.q: In the from-scratch code, what do Q, K and V represent?
options: What I'm looking for, what I offer, and what I contribute if attended to
questions.explain: Scores are Q @ K.T scaled by sqrt(d_model), then softmaxed.

questions.q: What does each row of the attention weights satisfy?
options: It sums to 1, a distribution over all tokens
questions.explain: The output is a weighted average of all value vectors.

questions.q: Why use multi-head attention?
options: Parallel smaller attentions let the model attend to different kinds of relationships at once
questions.explain: d_model must be divisible by n_heads.

questions.q: Why do modern tokenizers rarely hit words they can't represent?
options: Rare words are split into known subword pieces instead of an out-of-vocabulary token
questions.explain: For example 'unfamiliarly' becomes un, ##familiar, ##ly.

questions.q: Why fine-tune a pretrained transformer rather than train from zero?
options: Nobody retrains a transformer from scratch for every task; Hugging Face provides pretrained models and a standard workflow
questions.explain: The module covers tokenizers, loading a model and fine-tuning for classification.

questions.q: What does torch.no_grad() do during inference?
questions.explain: It's used while computing logits.

questions.q: What does the lesson use for the fine-tuning dataset size?
options: A shuffled subset: 2000 training and 500 test IMDB reviews
questions.explain: Small subsets keep the example fast.

questions.q: Which two methods does a custom Dataset require?
questions.explain: DataLoader handles batching, shuffling and parallel loading.

questions.q: What does num_workers > 0 do?
options: Loads data in parallel background worker processes so the GPU isn't waiting on I/O
questions.explain: It keeps the GPU fed.

questions.q: What does CosineAnnealingLR do?
options: Smoothly decays the learning rate along a cosine curve toward 0 over T_max epochs
questions.explain: No manual step-function tuning is needed.

questions.q: When is scheduler.step() called in the example?
options: Once per epoch, after all batches
questions.explain: The learning rate falls from 1e-2 toward 0.

questions.q: Why track experiments with MLflow?
options: You can't compare 40 runs by memory; logging makes them reproducible and comparable
questions.explain: It logs parameters, metrics and artifacts.

questions.q: What does each start_run() create?
options: A new, independently addressable record of params, metrics and the model, timestamped
questions.explain: Runs live inside a named experiment.

questions.q: How do you view the recorded runs?
questions.explain: The lesson prints this hint.

questions.q: What does client.search_runs(..., order_by=["metrics.accuracy DESC"]) return?
options: Past runs sorted by accuracy, best first
questions.explain: It lets you query runs programmatically.

questions.q: Why isn't git alone enough for ML projects?
options: Multi-gigabyte datasets and model checkpoints aren't cheap to diff
questions.explain: DVC tracks large files and stores lightweight pointers in git.

questions.q: What does data/train.csv.dvc contain?
options: A small pointer: a content hash and size, tracked by git
questions.explain: The actual file lives in the DVC remote, fetched with dvc pull.

questions.q: What does dvc repro run?
options: Only the stages whose dependencies changed since the last run
questions.explain: Stages declare deps, outs, params and metrics in dvc.yaml.

questions.q: Why pin versions in requirements.txt and use a Dockerfile?
options: 'Works on my machine' becomes 'works in this exact, reproducible container'
questions.explain: The same image runs on a laptop, CI and production.

questions.q: What is random search's blind spot?
options: Trial 50 learns nothing from trials 1–49, since samples are independent of past results
questions.explain: Bayesian optimization searches more intelligently.

questions.q: Why sample learning_rate with log=True?
options: The effect of 0.01 vs 0.02 is much larger than 0.20 vs 0.21
questions.explain: A log scale matches how learning rate matters.

questions.q: What does pruning do in Optuna?
options: Abandons a trial once it's clearly worse than the best so far, without finishing training
questions.explain: It monitors intermediate performance for iteratively trained models.

questions.q: What does direction="maximize" mean in the study?
options: Optuna seeks the highest objective value, here CV ROC AUC
questions.explain: The sampler is TPE with a seed for reproducibility.

questions.q: What do GPUs speed up in neural network training?
options: Large matrix multiplications, parallelized across thousands of cores
questions.explain: Every nn.Linear and attention Q @ K.T is a matmul.

questions.q: Why call torch.cuda.synchronize() when timing?
options: GPU ops are asynchronous, so you wait for completion before reading the clock
questions.explain: Otherwise timing would be wrong.

questions.q: Why does production code prefer DistributedDataParallel over DataParallel?
options: One process per GPU with no single bottleneck device, unlike DataParallel's gradient aggregation on one GPU
questions.explain: It's launched with torchrun --nproc_per_node=4.

questions.q: What is data parallelism?
options: Split the model layers across devices
Replicate the model and split the batch across devices
questions.explain: Each process handles a different data shard.

questions.q: What are the three standard compression techniques?
questions.explain: Fewer bits per number, fewer weights, and a smaller model taught to mimic a bigger one.

questions.q: What does quantize_dynamic do to Linear weights?
options: Converts 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers, cutting weight memory roughly 4x with usually minor accuracy loss
questions.explain: The int8 and fp32 outputs differ slightly but not zero.

questions.q: What does prune.l1_unstructured(layer, 'weight', amount=0.4) do?
options: Zeroes the smallest 40% of weights by magnitude
questions.explain: Small-magnitude weights contribute least to the layer's output.

questions.q: Why call prune.remove(layer, 'weight')?
options: To bake the mask in permanently and drop the pruning wrapper
questions.explain: It finalizes the pruned weights.

questions.q: What does an object detection model output?
options: A variable-length list of (box, label, score) triples
questions.explain: Unlike classification, it's one triple per detected object.

questions.q: What does semantic segmentation produce?
questions.explain: argmax(1) collapses the 21-channel score map to a class index per pixel.

questions.q: Why filter predictions with scores > 0.7?
questions.explain: It drops low-confidence boxes.

questions.q: What does IoU measure for a detected box?
options: Overlap between two boxes: intersection area over union area
questions.explain: The worked example computes it from box coordinates.

questions.q: Which paper's claim does the capstone reproduce?
options: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting (Srivastava et al., 2014)
questions.explain: Its central claim is testable in minutes.

questions.q: What is the claim being tested?
options: A network with dropout generalizes better (smaller train/test gap) than an identical one without it
questions.explain: Same data, architecture and optimizer.

questions.q: Why must the comparison keep everything else identical?
options: So any difference is attributable to dropout
questions.explain: The experiment uses the same seed, lr and epochs with dropout_p of 0.0 vs 0.5.

questions.q: Why call model.eval() when measuring accuracy?
options: To turn dropout off during evaluation
questions.explain: Dropout should only be active during training.

questions.q: What is training/serving skew?
options: The model is trained on one feature distribution but served another because of mismatched feature code
questions.explain: It is the single most common source of production ML failures.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what bug causes the skew?
options: The serving path substitutes a 90-day cached value for avg_purchase_30d
questions.explain: It happens with no error or crash.

questions.q: What is a feature store for?
options: Computing features consistently for both training and online lookup
questions.explain: It reduces the two-codebases problem.

questions.q: What closes the loop in the production architecture?
options: Online monitoring and feedback into new training data
questions.explain: Predictions feed back into monitoring.

questions.q: What does pydantic do in the FastAPI serving example?
options: Validates the request shape and types, returning a clear 422 for malformed requests before they reach the model
questions.explain: PredictRequest and PredictResponse define the schema.

questions.q: Why export a model to ONNX?
options: Portable, optimized inference that runs from Python, C++ or mobile without PyTorch installed
questions.explain: ONNX Runtime applies framework-agnostic optimizations like operator fusion.

questions.q: What does dynamic_axes batch_size allow?
options: The exported model to accept varying batch sizes
questions.explain: It marks the batch dimension as variable.

questions.q: What is the point of batching requests?
options: Higher throughput by running several predictions together within a max size and wait time
questions.explain: BatchPredictor uses max_batch_size and max_wait_ms.

questions.q: What does a feature store eliminate?
options: Duplicated feature logic: one definition computed once and served from batch (training) and low-latency (online) paths
questions.explain: It directly addresses training/serving skew.

questions.q: How do the offline and online stores differ?
options: Offline keeps full point-in-time history for training; online keeps only the current value per entity for live predictions
questions.explain: Each holds what its use case needs.

questions.q: What does the naive feature lookup do wrong for training?
options: It grabs the latest value, ignoring when the label happened, leaking the future
questions.explain: For a label on Jan 20 it returned 55.3 from Feb instead of 42.1.

questions.q: What is point-in-time correctness?
options: Using only feature values that existed before the label's timestamp
questions.explain: The lesson compares it to the rolling-window leakage bug.

questions.q: Why isn't code-only CI enough for ML?
options: ML fails in ways like silently dropped features, valid-but-worse models and shifting metric behavior
questions.explain: You also test data and model behavior.

questions.q: What does test_model_beats_naive_baseline check?
options: The model beats predicting the majority class by a margin
questions.explain: It asserts accuracy exceeds baseline + 0.05.

questions.q: What does the invariance test show?
options: Changing an irrelevant feature like customer ID shouldn't change predictions
questions.explain: It compares predictions before and after perturbing the ID.

questions.q: What does the no-regression test guard against?
options: Deploying a retrained model that is worse than the production model
questions.explain: It allows at most a 0.01 drop in accuracy.

questions.q: Why can a model that passed every CI gate still degrade?
options: The world keeps changing after deployment while the model stays frozen
questions.explain: You need monitoring and drift detection.

questions.q: Why log features, predictions and model version at prediction time?
options: Without the actual production inputs, drift detection is impossible after the fact
questions.explain: You compare production inputs to the training distribution.

questions.q: What does PSI measure?
options: How much a feature's production distribution has shifted from the training distribution
questions.explain: PSI < 0.1 means no significant drift; 0.1–0.25 moderate; above that is serious.

questions.q: What does 'close the loop' mean here?
options: Automated retraining triggers when drift is detected
questions.explain: Detect statistically, not by gut feel.

questions.q: Why assign variants by hashing (user_id, experiment_name)?
options: It's stateless, stable per user, and gives independent splits across experiments
It gives equal users to all
questions.explain: The experiment name acts as a salt.

questions.q: Why compute required sample size before launching?
options: To know how long the test must run and whether the effect is even detectable at your traffic
questions.explain: The example needs 14,057 users per variant for a 1pp lift at 80% power.

questions.q: What is the risk of early peeking?
options: Fooling yourself with significance you don't actually have
questions.explain: The lesson stresses reading results without overclaiming.

questions.q: What do alpha=0.05 and power=0.8 mean in sizing?
options: 5% false-positive tolerance and 80% chance to detect the true effect
questions.explain: They set the z values used in the sample-size formula.

questions.q: What is demographic parity?
options: Equal true positive rates among those who should be approved
questions.explain: Equal opportunity is equal true positive rates.

questions.q: Why does a fairness report compute both demographic parity and equal opportunity?
options: They're different, sometimes mutually exclusive, definitions: a model can satisfy one and violate the other
questions.explain: The lesson doesn't pick one number to optimize.

questions.q: How can an accurate model still fail?
options: It can systematically fail a subgroup, leak information about individuals, or be tricked by a crafted input
questions.explain: These are things you compute and test, not just ethics theory.

questions.q: What does the Laplace mechanism in differential privacy do?
options: Adds calibrated noise scaled by sensitivity and epsilon
questions.explain: It is the lesson's basic mechanics of differential privacy.

questions.q: What variable does this module target compared with Module 02?
options: Total infrastructure cost per served prediction, rather than per-request latency
questions.explain: It uses quantization, distillation and caching.

questions.q: What did int8 dynamic quantization achieve in the example?
questions.explain: The accuracy cost must be validated, not assumed negligible.

questions.q: What does the distillation loss combine?
options: Matching the teacher's soft output distribution (KL divergence) and getting the true label right
questions.explain: alpha weights the distill term; temperature softens the distributions.

questions.q: Why multiply the distillation term by temperature**2?
options: To keep gradient magnitudes comparable after softening
questions.explain: It's part of the standard formulation used in the lesson's code.

questions.q: What is an ML platform?
options: Shared infrastructure that lets many teams train, serve and monitor many models without reinventing the basics
questions.explain: It standardizes a model registry, self-serve training/serving and multi-tenant isolation.

questions.q: What does a model registry provide?
options: A single source of truth for what's deployed where
questions.explain: Instead of a spreadsheet or a teammate's memory.

questions.q: What happens to the old production version when a new one is promoted?
options: It's moved to ARCHIVED; only one PRODUCTION version at a time
questions.explain: The promote method enforces this.

questions.q: What stage does a newly registered model start in?
questions.explain: register() creates it as STAGING.

questions.q: What service does the capstone build?
questions.explain: It's trained, tested, served, drift-monitored, CI/CD-gated and A/B tested.

questions.q: What does the /score endpoint log for each prediction?
options: Timestamp, model version, features and fraud probability, for later drift detection
questions.explain: It appends JSON lines to prediction_log.jsonl.

questions.q: When is a transaction flagged?
questions.explain: flagged = proba > 0.5.

questions.q: Why does train.py use a stratified split and fixed seeds?
options: Reproducible training that preserves class balance
questions.explain: It follows the reproducible pattern from earlier modules.

questions.q: What shape does `np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])` have?
questions.explain: 2 rows and 3 columns; shape is the most-checked property in ML code.

questions.q: For `M = np.array([[1., 2., 3.], [4., 5., 6.]])`, what does `M.mean(axis=0)` return?
questions.explain: axis=0 goes down the columns, giving one mean per column.

questions.q: Which line is leakage-free?
options: `pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression())]); cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5)`
questions.explain: Inside a Pipeline the scaler is re-fit on each fold's training portion only.

questions.q: You evaluate a 1-nearest-neighbor model on its own training set and get 100%. What does it tell you?
options: Nothing: it memorized the data; evaluate on held-out data
questions.explain: A model can simply memorize training data.

questions.q: Which call keeps the class ratio the same in train and test?
questions.explain: stratify=y preserves class proportions.

questions.q: A fraud model has 3% positives. It scores 97% accuracy by predicting 'no fraud' always. What should you use instead?
options: Precision/recall and PR curves, with a deliberately chosen threshold
questions.explain: Accuracy lies on imbalanced data.

questions.q: Which technique may you apply to the test set when handling imbalance?
options: None: resampling is only for the training set
questions.explain: The test set must keep real-world class proportions.

questions.q: k-means with k=4 gives inertia 942.3 and with k=5 gives 868.7, after 3673.8 at k=3. What does the elbow suggest?
options: k=4, because improvements level off after it
questions.explain: Big drops until k=4, then marginal gains.

questions.q: You fit a `StandardScaler` before `KMeans` because...
options: k-means is pure distance math, so feature scale would dominate
questions.explain: Unscaled large-range features dominate distances.

questions.q: Which metric tells you how much of the target's variance a regression explains?
questions.explain: R² compares your model with predicting the mean.

questions.q: A random forest differs from plain bagging because it...
options: considers only a random subset of features at each split
questions.explain: That extra randomness decorrelates the trees.

questions.q: Gradient boosting differs from a random forest because...
options: trees are built sequentially, each correcting the errors so far
questions.explain: Boosting fits residuals step by step.

questions.q: For time-series features you write `df['sales'].shift(1).rolling(7).mean()`. Why shift(1)?
options: So the feature for day t only uses data before day t
questions.explain: An unshifted rolling window includes today's own target value, leaking the label.

questions.q: You split a daily-sales dataset for forecasting. Which split is valid?
options: Train on earlier dates, test on later dates (TimeSeriesSplit)
questions.explain: A random split lets the model train on the future.

questions.q: In PyTorch, `w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True); loss = (w - 5) ** 2; loss.backward()` leaves `w.grad` equal to...
In a training loop, what is the correct order inside each step?
questions.explain: Clear gradients, compute new ones, then update the weights.

questions.q: Why freeze the backbone with `requires_grad = False` in transfer learning?
options: So only the new head trains and the pretrained features are kept
questions.explain: Only the new final layer's parameters are updated.

questions.q: A teammate's serving code computes `avg_purchase_30d` differently from training. What is this called?
questions.explain: Duplicated feature logic in two code paths is a top production failure.

questions.q: Which tool compares the production distribution of a feature with its training distribution?
questions.explain: PSI above about 0.25 signals significant drift.

questions.q: You want to deploy a PyTorch model to run without PyTorch installed. What do you export to?
questions.explain: ONNX Runtime serves the model framework-independently.

challenges.title: Train/test split by hand
challenges.prompt: Without any libraries, split the list `data = list(range(10))` into a training list (first 80%) and a test list (last 20%) in order, as you would for time-ordered data, and print both lists.
challenges.starter:
data = list(range(10))
# split in order: first 80% train, last 20% test
# print(train) then print(test)
challenges.solution:
data = list(range(10))
cut = int(len(data) * 0.8)
train, test = data[:cut], data[cut:]
print(train)
print(test)
challenges.explain: For time-ordered data you split by position, never randomly, so the model never trains on the future.
